DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Did Christ have a biological father?

**Position.** No. The KJV says Jesus was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, with no man's seed involved. Joseph was his legal and reputed father, not his begetter. By "biological father" I mean a male parent who supplies the seed of conception. God is not a biological father in that sense: "God is a Spirit" (John 4:24), and "a spirit hath not flesh and bones" (Luke 24:39). [L1]

## 1. Matthew's genealogy changes its grammar at Joseph

"Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob" (Matt 1:2). The verb is repeated through Matt 1:2-16. [L1] The Greek is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "he begat", active, with the father as subject). [L2]

Then the pattern breaks: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus" (Matt 1:16). [L1] Two things change:

- The verb becomes ἐγεννήθη (egennēthē, "was born", passive). The active "begat" is dropped. [L2]
- The relative pronoun ἧς (hēs, "of whom") is feminine singular. It can refer only to Mary, not to Joseph. [L2]

Matthew calls Joseph "the husband of Mary" (ὁ ἀνήρ, ho anēr, "the husband/man"), not the father of Jesus. The unbroken "begat" line of Matt 1:2-15 stops at Joseph, and the child is traced to the mother alone. [L3, internal to the same chapter]

## 2. The stated source of the conception is the Holy Ghost, and Joseph is excluded

"When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost" (Matt 1:18). [L1]

- συνελθεῖν (synelthein, "to come together") is the marital union, and it is expressly placed after the conception. [L2]
- ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Spirit holy") names the source. ἐκ (ek, "out of") marks origin. [L2]

The angel tells Joseph: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matt 1:20). [L1] The Greek is τὸ γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ γεννηθὲν (to gar en autē gennēthen, "that which in her is begotten/conceived"), ἐκ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἁγίου (ek pneumatos estin hagiou, "is out of Spirit holy"). [L2] The same ἐκ marks the source in both verses.

Joseph's reaction confirms the reading. He was "minded to put her away privily" (Matt 1:19). He took the pregnancy as something that was not his, and the angel corrected only the question of its source. [L1]

Luke gives the same account from Mary's side:

- "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (Luke 1:34). The Greek is ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (andra ou ginōskō, "a man I know not"). [L1, L2]
- The answer: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God" (Luke 1:35). [L1]
- ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "will overshadow") describes a divine act. It is not the language of a husband's act. [L2]
- The word "therefore" (διό, dio, "wherefore") makes the divine, not human, conception the stated ground of the title "Son of God". [L2]

Two independent accounts, one to Joseph and one to Mary, agree. [L3]

## 3. The sign was a woman conceiving without a man

"Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel" (Matt 1:23, citing Isa 7:14). [L1]

- Isaiah's word is הָעַלְמָה (ha-'almah, "the young woman of marriageable age"). I do not rest the case on that word alone. [L2]
- Matthew's Greek is παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin"). The Spirit-given rendering fixes the meaning. [L2]
- The cross-reference: Rebekah is called a בְּתוּלָה (bethulah, "virgin") in Gen 24:16, "neither had any man known her". In Gen 24:43 the same woman is called הָעַלְמָה (ha-'almah). So the Hebrew word is used of a woman proved to be a virgin. [L1, L2, L3]
- Luke 1:27 ("a virgin espoused... and the virgin's name was Mary") together with Luke 1:34 fixes this particular woman's state before the conception. [L3]

A sign that a young wife conceived in the ordinary way would be no sign. It is a sign because no man was involved.

Matt 1:25 closes the matter: Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". ἐγίνωσκεν (eginōsken, "was knowing", in the sense of marital relations) is negated until after the birth. [L1, L2]

## 4. Joseph's fatherhood is reputed and legal, not biological

Luke 3:23: "Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." [L1] The Greek is ὡς ἐνομίζετο (hōs enomizeto, "as was supposed/reckoned"). The word is used for what people think, and it distinguishes the reputed relationship from the real one. [L2]

Objections I expect:

- **Luke 2:48** ("thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing") and **John 6:42** ("the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know"). John 6:42 is the crowd's statement, and Luke 3:23 has already told the reader it is a supposition. Luke 2:48 is Mary's wording in the household. Luke 2:49 immediately gives the child's answer: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" [L1] This is correction by the text itself, and Luke 2:33 and 2:41 use "his parents" in the same legal-household sense. [L3]
- **"Born under the law."** Gal 4:4 reads "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman". The Greek is γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come to be out of a woman"). Only the woman is named as the source, with no ἐκ ἀνδρός (ek andros, "out of a man"). [L1, L2] Compare Gen 3:15, "her seed", where the Hebrew זֶרַע (zera', "seed") is ordinarily spoken of the man's line. The promise is of the woman's seed. [L3]

## 5. The Davidic claim does not need Joseph's seed, and Joseph's seed would bar it

- Paul says Jesus was "made of the seed of David according to the flesh" (Rom 1:3). [L1] Peter says "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne" (Acts 2:30). [L1] Both say "according to the flesh" and neither names Joseph.
- Luke 3:23-31 traces a line to David through Nathan (Luke 3:31). Matthew's line runs through Solomon and Jechonias (Matt 1:6, 1:11-12). [L1]
- Of Coniah (Jechonias), God says: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David" (Jer 22:30; see Jer 22:24). [L1] The Hebrew is כִּי לֹא יִצְלַח מִזַּרְעוֹ אִישׁ (ki lo yitslach mi-zar'o ish, "for not shall prosper from his seed a man"). [L2]
- Gabriel tells Mary that "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David" (Luke 1:32). So a man of Jechonias's seed cannot sit on that throne, yet Jesus is to sit on it. [L3]
- [L4] Footing for this inference: (a) Matt 1:11-16 places Joseph in Jechonias's line, (b) Jer 22:30 bars Jechonias's seed from David's throne, and (c) Luke 1:32-35 gives the throne to the child conceived by the Holy Ghost. Taken together, Joseph's legal fatherhood gives the throne right through adoption into the line, while his seed would carry the curse. This does not require Joseph's seed, and on Jeremiah's words it excludes it.

## 6. "Only begotten of the Father" is a different kind of fatherhood

John 1:14: "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us... the glory as of the only begotten of the Father." [L1] The Greek is μονογενής (monogenēs, "only-born/unique"). [L2] Heb 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me" uses κατηρτίσω (katērtisō, "thou hast fitted/prepared"). [L1, L2] God prepared a body in Mary. He did not beget it as a man does. The Father in heaven is therefore Father by divine act, not by seed in the flesh. [L3]

---

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on:

1. Matthew's genealogy stops saying "begat" at Joseph and traces Jesus "of whom" (feminine) was "born" to Mary alone. Footing: Matt 1:2-16 [L1]; ἐγέννησεν/ἐγεννήθη (egennēsen, "begat"; egennēthē, "was born") and feminine ἧς (hēs, "of whom") [L2]; the contrast with Matt 1:2-15 [L3].
2. The conception was "of the Holy Ghost" before Joseph and Mary came together, and Mary says she knew no man. Footing: Matt 1:18, 1:20, Luke 1:34-35 [L1]; ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Spirit holy"), συνελθεῖν (synelthein, "to come together"), ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "will overshadow") [L2]; the agreement of Matthew's and Luke's separate accounts [L3].
3. The sign was a virgin conceiving, and Matt 1:25 confirms Joseph "knew her not" until after the birth. Footing: Isa 7:14, Matt 1:23, 1:25 [L1]; עַלְמָה/בְּתוּלָה (almah, "young woman"; bethulah, "virgin") and παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin") [L2]; Gen 24:16, 24:43, Luke 1:27 [L3].
4. Joseph was the supposed father, not the real one. Footing: Luke 3:23 [L1]; ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed") and γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come to be out of a woman") in Gal 4:4 [L2]; Luke 2:48-49, John 6:42, Luke 2:33 and Gen 3:15 read together [L3].
5. Davidic descent "according to the flesh" runs through the mother, and Joseph's own line carries the Jer 22:30 bar. Footing: Rom 1:3, Acts 2:30, Matt 1:11-16, Jer 22:30 [L1]; מִזַּרְעוֹ (mi-zar'o, "from his seed") [L2]; Luke 3:31 and Luke 1:32-35 [L3].
6. Jesus had no biological father. He was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, and God's fatherhood of him is by divine act and not by seed. Footing: links 1-5, John 1:14, Heb 10:5, John 4:24 [L1]; μονογενής (monogenēs, "only-born"), κατηρτίσω (katērtisō, "thou hast prepared") [L2]; Luke 24:39 together with Matt 1:20 [L3].

# Round 2: Defender's reply

The chain is what stands or falls (Isa 28:10), not any single word. I re-seat each pressed term in its chain.

## What the rebuttal leaves unanswered

- **Matt 1:19.** Joseph, "being a just man... was minded to put her away privily." This is his reaction to her pregnancy. [L1] If he were the begetter there would be nothing to put away privily. The angel answers only the question of source: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (Matt 1:20). [L1]
- **Luke 1:34.** "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" [L1] The rebuttal addresses verse 35's verbs. It does not address the words ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (andra ou ginōskō, "a man I know not"). [L2]
- **Matt 1:18.** "Before they came together, she was found with child." [L1] The challenger's own reading of Matt 1:25 is "abstinence during the pregnancy." Genesis 4:1 (the challenger's cited row) says "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived", so knowing precedes conceiving. Matt 1:25 says Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth." Conception falls inside that period. The challenger's two rows, pressed together, state my link 3. [L1, L3]

## Link 1: the naming act and John 6:42

- **Naming is not begetting.** Gabriel also says to Mary, "thou shalt call his name JESUS" (Luke 1:31). [L1] Mothers name children without a father's act: "Leah... called his name Reuben" (Gen 29:32), "Eve... called his name Seth" (Gen 4:25). [L1, L3] Joseph's naming at Matt 1:21, 25 is obedience and acknowledgment: he takes her (παραλαβεῖν, paralabein, "to take to oneself", Matt 1:20) and owns the child legally. [L2] That is the legal fatherhood I declared. It is not a seed claim.
- **John 6:42 is a claim about what the crowd knows.** Jesus answers the same crowd's wording in John 7:27-28: "we know this man whence he is... Ye both know me, and know whence I am: and I am not come of myself, but he that sent me is true." [L1] The crowd's "we know" is answered in the text by "ye know me, and know whence I am", followed by a source they do not know. [L3]
- **Matt 13:55 against Mark 6:3.** The same incident in Mark reads "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" [L1] Matthew's "the carpenter's son" (τοῦ τέκτονος υἱός, tou tektonos huios, "the craftsman's son") is a trade description in the town's mouth. Mark's version of the same speech names the mother alone. [L3]
- **The grammar break stands.** Thirty-nine actives are the pattern. The challenger's own count shows the one break falls at Matt 1:16, where the active is replaced and the relative is feminine (ἧς, hēs, "of whom"). [L1, L2] The pattern's departure at one point is the evidence. The passive does not need to say "no man begat him." The verb that every preceding line supplies is withheld.

## Link 2: ἐκ (ek, "out of") and the verb

- The challenger reads ek as "covenant origin." But the verb in Matt 1:20 is γεννηθέν (gennēthen, "begotten/conceived"), the same verb family as ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat") in Matt 1:2-16. [L2] The Holy Ghost is named as the source of the thing begotten, in the place where the genealogy puts a human father.
- John 1:13, the challenger's own row, sets ἐκ θεοῦ (ek theou, "out of God") against οὐδὲ ἐκ θελήματος ἀνδρός (oude ek thelēmatos andros, "nor out of the will of a man"). [L1, L2] In that verse ek-God and ek-man are alternatives. The challenger's row therefore does not show ek-God as compatible with ek-man. It sets them against each other.
- **Solomon (1 Chr 28:6; 2 Sam 7:14).** David begot Solomon by the stated ordinary means (2 Sam 12:24, "David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in unto her, and she bare a son"). [L1] God's "my son" is added to a known human begetting. In Matt 1:20 no human begetting is stated. Joseph is troubled by the pregnancy, and the angel supplies one source only. [L3]
- **Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34.** The same verb ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai, "shall come upon") is used of empowerment. [L2] But Luke 1:35 is the direct answer to "how shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The reply excludes a man's act by being the reply to that question, and it continues "that holy thing which shall be born of thee" (ἐκ σοῦ, ek sou, "out of thee"). [L1, L2] The text names only the mother as the source of the body. The "therefore" (διό, dio) joins the title to that conception. The throne gift in 1:32 and the conception in 1:35 are in one speech. [L1]

## Link 3: Isaiah's sign

- Matt 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled." [L1] "All this" is the conception by the Holy Ghost with no man. Matthew states the fulfilment. I do not need Isaiah 7:16 to carry it.
- **Isaiah 8:3 against 7:14.** Isaiah 8:3 states the ordinary means: "I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son." [L1] Isaiah 7:14 states no such act and calls the matter a sign from "the Lord himself" (7:14), after Ahaz was told to ask a sign "in the depth, or in the height above" (7:11). [L1] When Isaiah wants ordinary conception he says so. The challenger's own parallel shows the contrast. [L3, L4 resting on Isa 7:11, 7:14, 8:3 and Matt 1:22]
- **Almah and bethulah.** My opening already declined to rest on the word alone. [L2] Matthew's παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin") and Luke 1:27, 34 establish this woman's state. [L1]

## Link 4: ἐνομίζετο (enomizeto, "was supposed")

I do not adjudicate the verb in isolation. The same author uses the same verb family for suppositions that proved wrong:

- Luke 2:44, "supposing him to have been in the company" (νομίσαντες, nomisantes, "supposing"). The child was not there. [L1, L2]
- Acts 14:19, "supposing he had been dead" (νομίζοντες, nomizontes, "supposing"). He was not dead. [L1, L2]
- Acts 21:29, "whom they supposed that Paul had brought into the temple." He had not. [L1, L2]

Acts 16:13 reads "was wont", meaning customarily held. That fits: the verb is about what is held by people, and context settles whether it is true. Luke has just written 1:34-35 and 3:22. In the verse itself Luke adds "as was supposed" to "son of Joseph." [L3]

On Luke 3:38: "which was the son of God" is a "son of" by the Creator's making and without a human begetter, since Adam had no human father (Gen 2:7). [L1, L3] So the genitive τοῦ (tou, "of the") in Luke's list does not require begetting. The KJV prints "the son" in italics because the Greek has only "of." [L1, L2]

Luke 2:48-49: the juxtaposition is in the text. Mary says "thy father" (ὁ πατήρ σου, ho patēr sou). The child answers "my Father's business" (τοῦ πατρός μου, tou patros mou). [L1, L2] I claim only that the answer names a different father at the very point the term was used.

Gal 4:4 and Gen 3:15. Noted. Not conceding here. Goes to review. The chain's weight on link 4 is Luke 3:23 with Luke 2:44, Acts 14:19 and 21:29, and Matt 1:18-25. It does not hang on Gal 4:4 alone.

## Link 5: Davidic descent and Jer 22:30

- **"Seed" does not mean a man's seed only.** The word is used of a woman: "If a woman have conceived seed" (Lev 12:2). [L1] The Hebrew is תַזְרִיעַ (tazria', "she yields seed"). [L2] "Sara herself received strength to conceive seed" (Heb 11:11), with σπέρματος (spermatos, "of seed"). [L1, L2] So the challenger's inference, that seed requires a man's loins, runs against Lev 12:2 and Heb 11:11.
- **Rom 1:3 and Gal 4:4 are one construction.** Rom 1:3 reads γενομένου ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυίδ (genomenou ek spermatos Dauid, "having come to be out of the seed of David"). Gal 4:4 reads γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "having come to be out of a woman"). Both use the verb ginomai (to come to be), and neither uses gennaō (to beget). [L1, L2] Heb 2:16 adds "he took on him the seed of Abraham" (ἐπιλαμβάνεται, epilambanetai, "takes hold of"), naming no begetter. [L1, L2] [L4: from Rom 1:3, Gal 4:4, Heb 2:16, Lev 12:2, Heb 11:11 and Luke 1:35 "of thee", the seed of David reaches the child by the woman.]
- **The text does not name Mary's father.** I do not claim a verse that does. Luke 3:23 reads "the son of Heli" with no "begat", while Matt 1:16 reads "Jacob begat Joseph." [L1] Two different fathers cannot both be begetters of Joseph in the same sense. Luke's list (Nathan, Luke 3:31) therefore uses a different relation. [L4 resting on Matt 1:16 against Luke 3:23, and on τοῦ with no begetting verb, Luke 3:38.]
- **Ezra 2:61.** The challenger's row reads "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai... and was called after their name." [L1] It shows a man reckoned under his wife's father's name. The reckoning "by the house of their fathers" (Num 1:2) is the rule, and Ezra 2:61 shows its exception. [L3]
- **Jer 22:30.** The challenger concedes the object is "sitting upon the throne." The bar is on the throne. Zerubbabel was "governor of Judah" (Hag 1:1), not a king sitting on David's throne. [L1] The challenger says the throne is "given" (Luke 1:32). If Jechonias's seed is barred by its own inheritance, a throne given by God to one not of that seed meets the bar. The challenger's point therefore supports link 5. [L3, L4 resting on Jer 22:30, Matt 1:12-16 and Luke 1:32-35.]

## Link 6: the dilemma "flesh must come from a man"

- **God makes flesh with no begetter.** "The Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground" (Gen 2:7), and Luke 3:38 calls that man "the son of God." [L1] "She... shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man" (Gen 2:23): flesh without a mother. [L1, L3] So "a spirit hath not flesh and bones" (Luke 24:39) does not imply that all flesh comes through a man. Scripture shows God forming flesh without a begetter. [L4 resting on Gen 2:7, 2:21-23, Luke 3:38 and Luke 24:39.]
- **Heb 2:14.** "He also himself likewise took part of the same." [L1] The Greek is μετέσχεν (meteschen, "took part in"). The text does not say "begotten by." [L2]
- **Monogenēs and Isaac.** Noted. Not conceding here. Goes to review. Link 6's weight is on Matt 1:18-25 and Luke 1:34-35, not on that word.
- **Ps 139:16 and Heb 10:5.** Not load-bearing. The chain rests on Matt 1:20 and Luke 1:35.

## Answer to the listed premises

1. **Sign.** Footing: Isa 7:11, 7:14, 8:3 and Matt 1:22. [L1, L3]
2. **Luke 2:48-49.** Footing: ὁ πατήρ σου / τοῦ πατρός μου, the adjacent words. [L1, L2]
3. **Mary's line.** Footing: Rom 1:3 with Gal 4:4 (ginomai ek), Lev 12:2, Heb 11:11 and Luke 1:32, 35. [L1, L2]
4. **Jer 22:30.** Footing: Matt 1:12-16, Jer 22:30 and Luke 1:32. [L1, L3]
5. **ἐνομίζετο.** Footing: Luke 2:44, Acts 14:19, Acts 21:29 and Luke 3:23. [L1, L2, L3]
6. **Father by divine act.** Footing: Matt 1:20 γεννηθέν ἐκ πνεύματος and Luke 1:35 ἐκ σοῦ, with Gen 2:7 and Luke 3:38. [L1, L2, L3]

The challenger's strongest rows (Rom 1:3, Acts 2:30) name David's seed according to the flesh. They do not name the man who supplied it, and they use ginomai, not gennaō. Matt 1:19, Luke 1:34, Matt 1:18, 1:20 and 1:25 stand against every reading that supplies a man.
